item.title: 🟠 phpAfterShell Explained: How Hackers Could Turn a PHP Session Flaw Into Code Execution
item.description:
Why this matters: Potentially urgent issue — confirm whether your environment is exposed.
PHP's default file-based session storage can be made to return objects an attacker chose, by cutting off a session write at the right moment. When combined with a second weakness, such as a suitable gadget chain in the app, those objects can allow the attacker to run code on the server. item.title: 🟠 Everything Is a Web Application, Including Your Firewall
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.
One of the early targets of PHP2Shell exploitation was the firewall. On October 28, Palo Alto Networks confirmed that attackers were exploiting the two PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet. Both flaws let anyone execute code on the web server without authentication. The disclosure itself went a little wrong.

item.title: 🟠 Java4Shell, NGINX2Shell and more: Why we are not at "Yellow", (Wed, Nov 18th)
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

About a month ago, we went to Infocon Yellow for the first time in a few years. We decided to address the php2shell vulnerability and alert our readers to its significant impact. Following php2shell, we had a number of vulnerabilities and events that may also have scored high enough to trigger an Infocon "Yellow" [infocon]. In the last few days, we had a major Microsoft 365 outage, a critical vulnerability in Java, and a critical vulnerability in NGINX, which was disclosed today.

item.title: 🟠 Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.
At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.
